Available ≠ Accessible · WIC

The work
of getting help

WIC helps families afford nutritious food. Follow one mother down two paths to see what the help changes—and how much work it takes to keep getting it.

By Megan Quigley

One mother. Two paths. Five years.

Same mother. Same baby.

Same mother. Same baby. My baby is here. He is crying. I am exhausted.

Everyone says to sleep when he sleeps. Apparently that is also when I’m supposed to do everything else.

For many families, using the card starts with a trip: more than a mile to a WIC store in a city, or more than ten miles in the countryside. Across the country, 40% of low-income families with young children live beyond those distances.

I’ve kept coming back. But how many families manage that? Researchers followed children who enrolled in 2013: only 43.5% participated consistently through four and a half years.

What the help can change.

Without WICWith WIC

The Healthy Eating Index

100 possible points for the whole pattern of eating.

Those groceries add up. But do they change what children eat? Researchers looked beyond the grocery bill and scored children’s overall diets on a 100-point scale.

8

Without WICWith WIC

The Healthy Eating Index

Continued into year 3
compared with WIC in year 1 only

At age three, children who stayed in WIC into their third year scored 3.6 points higher than those who only received it in year one.

8

Without WICWith WIC

The Healthy Eating Index

Continued into year 3
compared with WIC in year 1 only

The difference is modest, but it is visible across the overall diet. Continuing WIC was associated with better diet quality.

8

With WIC
Without WIC

Now he is five. The same birthday in both paths.

WIC can make nutritious food more affordable. But a benefit only helps when a family hears about it, enrolls, finds a store, buys the right foods, and manages to keep renewing.

Make that work easier: connect families directly to WIC when they receive Medicaid or have a baby; offer appointments and renewals that fit working lives; bring authorized stores closer; and make approved foods and checkout rules easier to understand. Help should be easier to start—and easier to keep.

Getting help should take less work.

Behind the story

Sources & methodology

Narrative and dialogue written for this project. Research, calculations, prices, and map data are documented below.

New York WIC: applying and using benefits

Income eligibility is only one component of WIC certification. See also New York WIC FAQs, MHHC’s current phone appointment options, and New York’s benefit-expiration guidance. Product illustrations are schematic.

Qualitative referral study · 2026

Ten participant interviewees recruited through a New Hampshire WIC agency; the broader study includes New Hampshire and Vermont staff. Interviews February–April 2024; 8 of 10 learned of WIC from family/friends. Not nationally representative.

USDA · 2023 eligibility and coverage

Tables 3.1, 3.5 and 3.7. Coverage = average-month participants divided by eligible people. 95% intervals: Vermont 65.1–94.2%, New York 61.0–63.8%, Louisiana 39.9–42.7%, national 54.5–57.6%. Age values are cross-sectional.

USDA · WIC retailer access, Table A.20

FY2022 retailers; 2015–2019 ACS low-income families with children under 5 are a proxy for WIC-eligible families. Convenient access is within 1 mile in urban areas or 10 miles in rural areas. Rounded table percentages used.

USDA · FY2026 produce allowance

October 1, 2025–September 30, 2026: $52/month fully breastfeeding; $26/month child. Illustration assumes 12 fully breastfeeding months plus 48 child months, continuous eligibility and constant FY2026 rates. Excludes other foods and the optional juice substitution. Not actual redemption, total WIC value, guaranteed savings, or forecast.

JAMA Network Open · benefit redemption

Southern California, November 2019–June 2023 records; children aged 0–3 at certification in November 2019–June 2022. 188,368 participants. Table 2: 254,506 of 365,738 fruit-and-vegetable certification periods redeemed at least 70% (69.6%); the complement is 30.4%. Unit is certification periods, not people or lost dollars.

USDA · Infant and Toddler Feeding Practices Study, Year 5

2013 enrollment cohort. Consistent participation refers to mother or child receipt during years 1 and 2 and subsequent observed months through 54 months. Weighted 43.5% consistent, 56.5% not consistent. Not a current national count or a renewal dropout estimate.

Borger et al. · WIC participation and diet quality

Adjusted observational comparison at age 3: participation in only the first year was associated with a 3.6-point lower Healthy Eating Index–2015 score than participation into the third year. Scale is 0–100. Does not establish causation.

The stock-up basket · prices and WIC rules

Walmart online listing snapshots accessed September 24–25, 2026. Total $64.08; eligible foods $23.97; own payment $40.11. Quantities are for a larger stock-up with pantry food already at home, not a nutritionally complete meal plan. Prices are not a local store quote. The linked ledger contains every item, quantity, unit price, product source, and food rule. Covered amounts assume sufficient corresponding benefits and an authorized store.

Artwork & approach

Original SVG character, environment, food, and chart drawings; OpenStreetMap road geometry; scroll-driven movement and receipt calculations. Inspired by character continuity in The Pudding’s Teenagers, conversational pacing in Middle School, and transaction-to-population storytelling in Yard Sale.
